summary_md:
Romero Moreno, Chakraborty and Brede (PLOS ONE 2021) study influence maximisation in a voter model with zealots. An active controller spreads a budget over the nodes of one 1,133-node university email network against a passive opponent whose allocation is fixed and known. They compare a discrete regime (K nodes at fixed gain) with a continuous regime (any intensity per node). The continuous optimum is spread out: about 111 of 1,133 nodes get above-average allocation, and the remaining mass is near uniform (std/mean 0.11). It beats the best discrete plan by 5-10% when the opponent targets fewer than 100 nodes.

Hub (degree) targeting explains discrete optima but explains little in the continuous regime. Two heuristics do: shadowing (spend where the opponent spends) and shielding (spend on the neighbours of the opponent's targets). Continuous shadowing plus shielding comes within 1.89e-3 of optimal vote share under budget advantage, against 2.09e-2 for degree targeting. In the low-allocation limit the best response is linear in the opponent's spend, with coefficient (Ba/Bb − 1): a richer controller shadows the opponent and a poorer one avoids the opponent's nodes. When both controllers optimise, the unique pure Nash equilibrium is uniform allocation. The paper uses no political data, no lobbying data and no noise.

The paper matters here because Melange's money layer is exactly this setup. optimize.py allocates a CU pot in $500 steps against fixed industry money, a passive opponent, and pflip is a single-node a/(a+b) vote-share form. In the system, though, money acts only on the funded member's own pflip and never spreads to neighbours, so shielding cannot emerge. An opponent-share field w_b already exists, labelled for a "shadowing layer", but no engine reads it. The contested-bills registry cites this paper for a counterparty term that no code uses yet. The paper's support is theoretical and comes from one network, so it supports the design concept and gives no calibration.

bearings.paper_claim: Against a passive opponent with known allocation w_b, the low-allocation optimum is w_ai linear in w_bi with coefficient c = (Ba/Bb − 1): shadow if Ba > Bb, avoid if Ba < Bb (Eq 5). Continuous shadowing+shielding comes within 1.89e-3 of the numerical optimum under budget advantage, against 2.09e-2 for degree targeting and 2.14e-2 for uniform. Under disadvantage it comes within 7.28e-4, against 2.12e-3 for discrete degree targeting (K=16, Fig 6).
bearings.system_side: The registry gives contested bills a per-bill counterparty set, but its docstring says 'no consumer exists today' (CONTESTED_V1 is a future dial). Separately, build_opposition_prior.py builds a per-member opposition share w_b that sums to 1.0, with consumer listed as 'coalition-builder adversary substrate / shadowing layer'. No engine file imports it (VERIFIED by searching fec/engine, moneyball_core.py and the templates for opposition_prior).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a design template: (1) the opponent's allocation is observed per member, which w_b approximates from FEC opposition money and not from LDA (D-021); (2) the opponent is passive within the planning horizon. The paper's dynamics are an unnoised voter model on an academic email network, so the coefficient (Ba/Bb − 1) and the gap sizes are not calibrated for Congress. Which side holds the budget advantage must be measured per bill before the sign of the response is chosen. UNVERIFIED for this system until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-lobbying#Contested-bills registry|Contested-bills registry]]

bearings.paper_claim: With a passive opponent, the continuous optimum spreads widely: |H|+|A| = 111 of 1,133 nodes above average, |V| = 1,013 near-flat (std/mean 0.11). It beats the best discrete plan by 5-10% for opponent K < 100. When two active controllers optimise simultaneously, the unique pure Nash equilibrium is uniform allocation (w_ai = Ba/N), whatever the network or budgets.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.5 Fig 1a (lines 285-308); p.6 Fig 1c (lines 337-345); p.13 (lines 758-782)
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy spends a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks with a $10k per-member cap. Industry money ind is fixed at fm.ind0 throughout, so industry is a passive opponent. The marginal of a chunk on member m changes only m's own pflip (marg_at sums tgt[m]·Δpflip over topics). CU dollars do not change neighbours' nA/nB, which are set by stance camps.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's spread and shielding results come from money propagating through the network's steady state. Melange's money term is node-local, so neither can arise in this optimizer; only shadowing-like behaviour through the b term of a/(a+b) can. The Nash result means the plan is a best response to a frozen opponent and could be exploited if industry PACs re-optimise. The paper's game is an idealised voter-model game, so this is a qualitative caution only. Equal-budget and per-candidate FEC limits have no analogue in the paper.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Joint CU budget optimizer|Joint CU budget optimizer]]

bearings.paper_claim: Steady-state opinion of node i in the voter model with zealots solves (L + Wa + Wb)x = wa. Each node's A-share is a ratio of A-pull (neighbours' state plus wa_i) to total pull (d_i + wa_i + wb_i) (Eq 1-2). In the high-allocation limit (w >> d) the optimum has no degree dependence (Eqs 7-8).
bearings.paper_location: Model p.3 Eq 1-2; Results pp.7-8 Eqs 7-8 (lines 487-539)
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a = WM·pm·saturating CU money + WP·nA/mAt and b mirrors it with industry money and anti neighbours. Neighbour pull comes from stance-labelled camps normalised by the network maximum. It is a one-shot ratio, not a self-consistent steady state.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The functional form is analogous: both are share-of-pull ratios. The paper's analytics need neighbour states to be endogenous; Melange fixes them from category_stance.json, so the paper's HMF results do not apply directly. The analogy supports reading pflip as a voter-model-style vote-share proxy, never as a vote or access probability (D-025).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Flip - winnability model|Flip - winnability model]]

bearings.paper_claim: The degree correlation of optimal allocations is a by-product of shielding: Kendall tau > 0.5 for K > 30 for both optimal and pure-shielding plans. When the opponent targets nodes with low-degree neighbours, |tau| for the optimum falls below 0.25 and shielding gives tau down to about −0.5 (Fig 5b-c). 'Optimal allocations can be explained almost perfectly by the shielding heuristics without the need for additional assumptions about degree preference' (p.11).
bearings.system_side: Diagnostic only, not consumed by the chain. It reports Spearman rho between Katz-Bonacich centrality on build_P and the optimizer allocation, money and score. It reads low rho as the allocator pricing stance, receptivity and leverage beyond centrality.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An allocation-centrality correlation, high or low, can come from where the opponent places money rather than from a preference for centrality. Any reading of rho should be stratified by industry-money placement, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED. Rho here is a heuristic diagnostic, not evidence of influence. The paper's evidence comes from one email network.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Katz-Bonacich benchmark (diagnostic)|Katz-Bonacich benchmark (diagnostic)]]

bearings.paper_claim: In the discrete regime (K nodes at fixed gain), optima are driven mainly by degree (hub targeting). Shadowing and shielding matter mostly in the continuous regime, and shielding weakens as the opponent spreads (K = 256).
bearings.system_side: The frontier and coalition engines pick discrete A seeds under a progressive two-colour first-to-reach IC race against fixed anti seeds, with bystanders turned by industry money. Lazy greedy runs up to 60 seeds with CRN draws.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The dynamics differ: IC is progressive (an activated node stays activated), while the voter model is reversible. Only the regime point carries over: seed-set optimisers will tend toward hubs, and opponent-aware placement matters more when allocation is continuous. Weak evidence; one network, no noise.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Competitive independent cascade with common random numbers|Competitive independent cascade with common random numbers]]

gaps_exposed: Money does not propagate in the flip model or the joint optimizer: CU dollars change only the funded member's pflip (optimize.py:64-72). The paper's main mechanism, shielding the neighbours of opponent-targeted nodes, therefore cannot appear in any allocation the system produces.

Opponent allocation is fixed (ind = fm.ind0 at optimize.py:59), so the allocator best-responds to a frozen opponent. The system has no test of how its plan fares if industry PACs re-optimise; the paper's two-active-controller result says that equilibrium is uniform allocation.

An opponent-share field w_b (build_opposition_prior.py:1425-1440) is labelled for a 'shadowing layer', and contested_bills.py ships a counterparty registry, but no engine consumes either (contested_bills.py:9 says 'no consumer exists today').

The paper says the direction of the best response depends on budget ratio Ba/Bb. The system never computes per-bill or per-topic CU vs counterparty budget ratios, so it cannot tell whether shadowing or avoidance would apply.

The paper's exploitability result (Eq 6) says a non-uniform opponent is most exploitable on low-degree nodes. The system has no diagnostic of where industry money departs from uniform relative to network degree.
flags: Citation scope: contested_bills (Paul's position list) cites 'Romero Moreno 2021' for a counterparty term. The paper is an abstract, unnoised voter model on one 1,133-node academic email network, with no lobbying, election or legislative data. It supports the concept of an opponent-aware allocation, not any parameter or effect size.

D-025 wording: the paper's 'influence' and 'vote share' are steady-state model outputs. Any shadowing or shielding score built from it must be described as a heuristic model output, not closeness, access or the probability of a vote.
D-021: an opponent allocation w_b for shadowing must come from FEC money (as build_opposition_prior.py's basis does), never from LDA spend used as a weight.
DE-062: the claim that emergent shadowing would follow from the b term of a/(a+b) in the optimizer is this agent's inference. It is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.
The paper's internal inconsistency (|Z| = 9 at line 302 vs 7 at line 307) and its reliance on an unread S1 Appendix for other topologies limit how far its generality claims can be relied on.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues neither for dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor for per-edge volume normalisation.
paul_alignment: This agrees with Paul's stated takeaway on contested bills: explicit inter-industry conflict over a bill is 'vital for political intelligence', and he wants rival industries modelled (Kim J. 2025 margin note). The paper gives that wish a formal shape: the response to a rival should depend on where the rival spends and on the budget ratio. It goes beyond his reading in two ways. First, the right response can be to avoid the rival's targets when CU is outspent. Second, a frozen-opponent plan is exploitable once the rival also optimises. His positions on the joint optimizer (adaptive greedy plus CELF, a learned policy later) do not mention opponent placement. They are therefore stale relative to what the system already holds: an unconsumed w_b 'shadowing layer' and an unwired registry. Neither the notes nor the system have taken up the paper's main mechanism, shielding, which the system's node-local money term cannot express.

related.why: Competitive influence maximisation in voter dynamics, adding timing and network heterogeneity, which addresses this paper's time-invariant-strategy limitation.
Competitive IC is the model behind the system's two-colour cascade race. This paper gives the voter-model (reversible) counterpart with an opponent-aware best response.
Competitive threshold models, which the flip model cites for having no submodularity guarantee. This paper instead proves concavity and a unique equilibrium in the continuous voter model.

Both derive equilibrium allocations across a network. B-P predict money loads on Katz-Bonacich centrality; this paper shows that a centrality correlation can be a by-product of the opponent's placement, which affects how kb_benchmark is read.
Both test whether simple heuristics approach optimised allocations; here shadowing and shielding outperform degree heuristics in the continuous regime.
Per-bill support and oppose positions by industry are the observed opponent placement that a shadowing response on contested bills would need.

backlinks.why: Romero Moreno is the stated basis for the contested-bills counterparty term. Pritoni supplies the empirical case that counterparties should be set per issue rather than globally.
Voter-dynamics influence maximization is an opinion-aware formulation of the kind the survey groups under opinion dynamics, and it is already cited for the contested-bills counterparty term.

meta.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians
meta.venue: Working paper, version 0.1 (no journal or DOI shown in the text; the metadata hint's "not visible" note is correct)

extraction.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians
extraction.venue: Working paper, version 0.1 (no journal or DOI shown in the text; the metadata hint's "not visible" note is correct)
extraction.document_type: Working paper / manuscript (version 0.1), about 48 pages of main text plus appendix
extraction.coverage: Full text read: lines 0 to 5066 of the text file (EOF reached), covering abstract, introduction, Study 1 to Study 4 (method and results), discussion, limitations, use cases, conclusion, references, general appendix, Study 1 literature overview, Study 2 and Study 3 appendices. No Paul markup files were listed for this item ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Nothing in the text concerns lobbying, legislative networks, path-finding, allocation, or text-as-data pipelines beyond literature mentions and one use-case paragraph; the only text-measurement point is the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) computer-assisted content analysis reference.
extraction.research_question: How can political personality be assessed with a comprehensive, facet-level, contextualized, psychometrically validated inventory that works for (a) voters' ideal traits for politicians, (b) citizens' perceptions of actual politicians' traits, and (c) perceived self-other similarity between voters and politicians? (p.2, p.11-12)
extraction.theory: Bottom-up construction of 15 politically relevant personality facets, each located a posteriori in the nomological net of established models: NEO PI-R, BFI-2, IPIP-NEO (Big Five facets), HEXACO, Values-in-Action character strengths, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" (Abele et al., 2020), and the six-category political leadership trait scheme of Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) (Table 1, pp.14-16). Argues global frameworks (Big Five, Big Two) lack specificity and contextualization, while ad hoc political measures lack generalizability and create jingle/jangle problems (pp.4-6). Argues contextualized items referring to the political role outperform non-contextualized ones (Danner and Lechner, 2024; Shaffer and Postlethwaite, 2012) and that items should target observable behavioral cues because voters judge the public persona (pp.8-10). Flags ideological content in items (Hatemi and Verhulst, 2015) and social desirability bias (Backstrom et al., 2009) as threats to neutrality (pp.9-10).
extraction.data: Four German-language survey studies, unit = individual respondent rating self, an ideal politician, or a named real politician. Study 1 (pp.11-14, Table 1): no data sample; literature mapping and item pool construction (110-item pool). Study 2 (self-ratings, general population, pp.22-26): N = 404 after excluding 21 straight-liners (fieldwork Oct 2020; Respondi AG online panel, CAWI; German native speakers; quotas on age, gender, education from German census; 51.0% female; age M = 42.6, SD = 14.0, range 18-68; education 34.9% low, 33.2% intermediate, 31.9% high). Study 3 (other-ratings of ideal politician, pp.27-28): N = 589 after excluding 40 straight-liners (fieldwork May 2020; same sampling as Study 2; randomized male-politician (N = 289) vs female-politician (N = 300) prompts; 51.3% female; age M = 43.4, SD = 14.6, range 18-69). Study 4 (observer ratings of real politicians, pp.29-34): N = 211 after excluding 2 straight-liners (clickworker.de crowdsourcing, fieldwork April 2021; EUR 2.25 compensation; Trump n = 104, Merkel n = 107; 38.9% female; age M = 39.9, SD = 13.3, range 18-69; education 4.7% low, 19.0% intermediate, 76.3% high; authors describe sample as male-leaning, highly educated, and somewhat left-leaning). Study 2 used 110-item pool, planned missingness (three partial blocks A/B/C plus common block X, each respondent 85 of 110 items); Study 4 used 86 personality items plus catch-all candidate measures.
extraction.method: Item construction from explicit facet definitions with two disambiguating trait words per item and balanced positive/negative keying (pp.21-22). 5-point agreement scale (Study 2, 3) and 1-5 scale for facet composites (Study 4). Composite facet scores are prorated means of 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice uses 2 items). Factorial validity: principal components analysis of ipsatized items (centered on each respondent's mean to remove acquiescence) with Horn (1965) parallel analysis, 1,000 random draws, run in Stata fapara (pp.24-25, 28, 30). Reliability: Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability omega from a CFA congeneric model (Raykov, 1997), Stata sem/relicoef (pp.25, 28, 30). Convergent validity: correlations of facet composites with BFI-2-XS domain scores and a three-item Machiavellianism scale (Study 2, Table 3); Study 4 correlations with catch-all candidate measures on 11-point scales (likeability feeling thermometer, vote propensity, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness, left-right placement and absolute ideological proximity). Group comparisons: Cohen's d for male vs female prompt (Study 3) and Trump vs Merkel means (Study 4), plus sociodemographic means (Table A3). PCA reported with orthogonal varimax rotation for the prototype and candidate composites (Figures A4, A7).
extraction.identification: None stated. The paper is psychometric and descriptive: cross-sectional survey correlations, mean differences, and factor structure. It does not claim causal identification. The text calls the Study 4 correlations "predictive validity" (p.36), but the analyses are concurrent associations among same-occasion ratings (Table 5).
extraction.scope: Population: German native-speaking adults in general population panels (Studies 2-3) and German native-speaking crowdsourced raters (Study 4). Institutional focus: individual politicians as perceived by voters; item wording references the political role. Targets in Study 4: Donald Trump (US former president) and Angela Merkel (German former chancellor). Era: fieldwork 2020-2021; the paper's literature runs to 2024. Language: German items with English translations in Table A2. The authors note that generalization to lesser-known politicians and to other countries is untested (p.38).

key_findings.finding: The framework has 15 politically relevant personality facets (e.g., Trust & Faith in Others; Compromise & Cooperativeness; Assertiveness & Will to take control; Dedication & Sacrifice), each mapped to HEXACO, Big Five, VIA, Agency/Communion, and the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) traits.
key_findings.numbers: 15 facets; 4-item scales plus one 2-item scale (Dedication & Sacrifice)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated facet reliabilities (Study 2) were moderate to high for most facets but low for several.
key_findings.numbers: alpha .44-.87; omega .43-.84. Lowest: Loyalty to Principles alpha .44 / omega .46; Humility alpha .46 / omega .43; Compromise alpha .51 / omega .45. Highest: Dedication alpha .87 / omega .84 (2-item scale)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated facets converge with the expected Big Five domains in the BFI-2-XS (Study 2): trust, compromise and empathy track Agreeableness; passion tracks Extraversion; optimism and composure track Emotional Stability.
key_findings.numbers: Trust-A r = .50; Empathy-A r = .48; Compromise-A r = .33; Passion-E r = .57; Optimism-ES r = .63; Self-Confidence-ES r = .56; Manners-C r = .59; Creativity-O r = .33. Machiavellianism: Integrity r = -.44, Empathy r = -.44, Humility r = -.37

key_findings.finding: Intellect & Mental Acuity correlated unexpectedly with BFI-2 Emotional Stability, mostly driven by one depression item.
Essential unidimensionality for most facets in self-ratings, with Creativity & Problem-Solving the clear exception and Loyalty to Principles borderline.
key_findings.numbers: Horn parallel analysis retained one component for all facets except Creativity; 15 scales judged essentially unidimensional

key_findings.finding: Ideal-politician prototypes showed almost no dependence on the politician's gender. Only Assertiveness differed, and it was rated more desirable for a female politician.
key_findings.location: Study 3 results, p.28; Table A5, p.74
key_findings.numbers: |d| = .00-.19; Assertiveness d = .19, p = .025 (male N = 289, female N = 300)

key_findings.finding: Ideal-trait scale reliabilities were modest. Assertiveness yielded two factors because one item (power-hungry, claims leadership) loaded reversed.
key_findings.numbers: Text: alpha .40-.78, omega .55-.79. Table A4 gives alpha .53-.78 with Assertiveness not computed (n.c.)

key_findings.finding: Observer ratings of Trump and Merkel differed significantly on 14 of 15 facets. The clearest contrasts were Self-Confidence & Composure, Trust & Faith in Others, and Humility, with Trump lower; Trump was rated higher on Assertiveness, Passion, and Creativity. Loyalty to Principles showed no difference.
key_findings.numbers: Self-Confidence d = -3.31 (Trump M 1.80 vs Merkel M 4.20); Trust d = -2.15 (1.72 vs 3.23); Humility d = -3.27 (1.31 vs 3.69); Assertiveness d = 1.41 (4.12 vs 3.33); Passion d = .93 (3.55 vs 2.73); Creativity d = .45 (2.98 vs 2.63); Loyalty d = .00 (3.31 vs 3.31); Trump N = 104, Merkel N = 107

key_findings.finding: Facets correlate with catch-all candidate measures in theoretically expected ways. Compassion tracks likeability; Integrity and Honesty tracks honesty; general assertiveness tracks the Assertiveness facet.
key_findings.numbers: Empathy-likeability r = .70 (Trump) / .76 (Merkel); Integrity-honesty r = .70 / .80; Assertiveness-general assertiveness r = .42 / .53; Passion-charisma r = .58 / .61 (Trump / Merkel); Intellect-vote propensity r = .67 (Trump); Creativity-vote propensity r = .71 (Merkel)

key_findings.finding: Ideological proximity to the target correlates with several facet ratings, consistent with political opponents attributing more undesirable traits. The authors interpret this as bias in observer ratings.
key_findings.location: Table 5 column Prx, pp.33-34; text pp.32-33
key_findings.numbers: Intellect-proximity r = .48 (Trump); Integrity-proximity r = .46 (Trump) and .36 (Merkel); Creativity-proximity r = .37 (Merkel)

key_findings.finding: Observer ratings of Trump and Merkel were reported to show a reliability range that does not match Table A7 for two facets.
key_findings.numbers: Text: alpha .40-.93, omega .48-.94. Table A7 lists Loyalty to Principles alpha .34 (omega n.c.) and Assertiveness alpha .40 / omega .48. Loyalty may be bidimensional in observer ratings (footnote 5, p.30)

key_findings.finding: Study 2 Discussion states the Study 1 item pool was reduced to four core items per facet (60 total). The Study 2 section describes 58 retained items (14 four-item scales plus one two-item scale).
key_findings.numbers: 58 vs 60 items; 110-item initial pool

measures: 15 PoliPers facets, self-report and observer versions, with 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice: 2 items); 5-point agreement scale (Studies 2-3), 1-5 composites (Study 4)
Opposite poles defined per facet, e.g., Reserve & Reluctance to Trust; Rigidity & Inflexibility; Apathy & Indifference (pp.17-21)
BFI-2-XS (Rammstedt et al., 2018) domain scores for convergence (Study 2)
Three-item Machiavellianism scale (Moshagen et al., 2020) for convergence (Study 2)

Catch-all candidate measures in Study 4, 11-point scales from AUTNES 2013 and GLES-style items: left-right placement (with absolute ideological proximity), likeability (feeling thermometer), propensity to vote, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness (Table A8 wordings, pp.74-76)
Ipsatized composite scores; Cronbach alpha and composite omega (Raykov, 1997)
limitations: Social desirability and ideological bias may affect both self-reports and observer ratings (p.37, citing Rothschild et al., 2019).
Reliance on survey data restricts applicability; longitudinal, experimental, and qualitative designs are called for (pp.37-38).

Study 4 raters' affect toward the targets may drive ratings; Trump and Merkel are polarizing figures, and the authors separate positivity from descriptive normativity (p.38, citing Wessels et al., 2020).
Lesser-known politicians are untested (p.38).

Study 2 and Study 3 use general-population samples with neutralized wording ('other people' instead of 'other politicians'; 'work' instead of 'politics') (p.22), so the instrument has not been validated on actual politicians as self-raters.
Study 4 sample is skewed: 76.3% high education, 38.9% female, male-leaning, somewhat left-leaning (p.29).
Dedication & Sacrifice was tested with only two positively worded items and is 'yet to become fully fledged' (p.21).
Several 4-item scales have low reliability (alpha .44-.52 for Loyalty, Humility, Compromise, Creativity in Study 2; Table 2, p.25).
Assertiveness and Loyalty show multidimensionality or reversed items (pp.28-30).
Predictive validity is claimed in the Discussion (p.36) but the evidence is concurrent correlations only.

Inconsistent study labels: Table 2 and Table 3 are labeled Study 1 while the data are from Study 2; Table 4 and Table 5 are labeled Study 3 while the data are from Study 4; the Study 3 section heading is used for the ideal-trait study whereas the discussion labels it Study 3 too. Readers must map labels by content.
Acquiescence control relies on ipsatization and balanced keying; the authors do not report a model-based acquiescence correction.

summary_md:
PoliPers is a working paper (version 0.1, not peer reviewed) that builds a survey inventory of 15 politically relevant personality facets. Examples are Trust & Faith in Others, Compromise & Cooperativeness, Assertiveness & Will to Take Control, Empathy & Compassion, and Integrity & Honesty. Each facet is mapped to the Big Five, HEXACO, VIA, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" and the Aaldering-Vliegenthart leadership traits. The authors test it in four German samples: self-ratings (N=404), ideal-politician ratings (N=589) and crowd ratings of Trump and Merkel (N=211).

Reliability is uneven. Self-rating alphas run from .44 to .87, and Loyalty, Humility and Compromise all fall at or below .51. Assertiveness splits into two factors: the "power-hungry, claims leadership" item loads reversed in ideal ratings, and observer-rating alpha is .40. Observer ratings carry a large evaluative component. Empathy correlates with likeability at r=.70/.76 and Integrity with rated honesty at .70/.80. Rated facets also correlate with the rater's ideological proximity to the target, for example r=.46 between Integrity and proximity for Trump. The paper calls these "predictive validity", but all of them are concurrent associations measured on the same occasion.

The paper matters here because it is the upstream source of the two facet labels in Paul's agency/communion persona codebook (fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py), which feeds the receptivity layer at PERSONA_W 0.30. It does not test how personality affects response to pressure, lobbying, cosponsorship or votes. Its evidence therefore bears on how the persona construct is defined and on rater-bias risks. It gives no support to the susceptibility signs the engine assigns. It also supports two existing design choices: de-identifying text before LLM rating, and modeling halo as a method factor. Transfer is limited by the setting: German raters, two very prominent leaders, and the 2020-21 era.

bearings.paper_claim: Defines 15 PoliPers facets, including Assertiveness & Will to take control (mapped to Agency) and Empathy & Compassion (mapped to Communion), each with a defined opposite pole such as Apathy & Indifference.
bearings.paper_location: Study 1, Table 1, pp.14-16; facet definitions pp.17-21
bearings.system_side: The persona codebook labels its two cue classes with exactly these PoliPers facet names (agency = 'Assertiveness & Will to Take Control', communion = 'Empathy & Compassion'). It reaches them through Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025 and scores positive poles only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The facet definitions transfer as construct definitions. The psychometric evidence does not: it comes from German survey ratings, not from LLM coding of English congressional text. PoliPers validates the facets as rated traits, not as sentence-level cues.

bearings.paper_claim: The Assertiveness facet is not unidimensional. In ideal-politician ratings it yielded two factors because the 'power-hungry, claims leadership' item loaded reversed (alpha not computed). In observer ratings of Trump and Merkel its alpha was .40 and omega .48. Ideal-rating Assertiveness was the only facet that differed by politician gender (d=.19).

bearings.system_side: The self-test treats 'I claim leadership and I am not afraid to use power to get results' as a gold agency unit. All agency cues, including power-seeking ones, are pooled into a single agency share.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies wherever agency is read as a single construct. The paper's evidence comes from survey items rated by citizens, so whether power-claiming cues also split from leadership-taking cues in congressional text is untested. That makes this a plausibility warning, not a measured defect.

Integrity correlates with ideological proximity at .46 (Trump) and .36 (Merkel), and Intellect with proximity at .48 (Trump). The paper tests no link from any facet to behavior under pressure.

The sign and weight of the persona term remain owner design priors (PERSONA_W is kept by owner ruling), and nothing in this paper validates or refutes them.

bearings.paper_claim: Observer ratings of politicians are biased by the rater's ideological proximity (r=.36-.48 on Integrity, Intellect and Creativity) and dominated by global evaluation (facet-likeability r up to .76). The authors interpret this as bias and separate positivity from descriptive normativity.

bearings.system_side: Senate expert and insider panels are treated as independent gold criteria. A halo PC1 bifactor removal (P2) was tested against the panel.

bearings.paper_claim: Global Big Five domains lack specificity for politics, and contextualized facet measures outperform non-contextualized ones. Facets diverge within a domain: for example, Compromise correlates with Agreeableness at r=.33 while Trust correlates at .50, and Intellect correlates unexpectedly with Emotional Stability at .41.

bearings.transfer_conditions: The argument concerns survey item design, not text features. A facet-level text reader would need its own validation, and the existing domain-level validity record (A-ES halo, O reversed on the party check) is not changed by this paper.

gaps_exposed: The persona channel collapses PoliPers' 15 facets into 2 cue shares. Facets with the most face relevance to lobbying receptivity have no measure: Compromise & Cooperativeness, Trust & Faith in Others, and Integrity & Honesty. Compromise is approximated only behaviorally, by cooperation_v2.
Opposite poles (indifference, distrust, rigidity) are coded as 'none' rather than as negative evidence, so low communion and missing communion cues are indistinguishable.
There is no check of whether the gold validation panels' ratings track rater partisanship or ideological proximity, which the paper shows contaminates observer trait ratings.

The assumption that the projected persona is what a lobbyist meets is untested. PoliPers measures persona as perceived by voters, and nothing in the system measures how lobbyists or staff perceive members.
The agency construct is not checked for the leadership-claiming versus power-seeking split that PoliPers found in Assertiveness.
flags: Working paper version 0.1, not peer reviewed, with inconsistent study labels and item counts (58 vs 60). Cite with that status.
The paper's 'predictive validity' wording (p.36) describes same-occasion concurrent correlations. Do not quote it as predictive evidence for any member-level forecast.

Nothing in the paper validates the receptivity persona signs (communion means susceptible, agency means resistant). The persona term stays a design prior. PERSONA_W 0.30 is kept by owner ruling, and this paper is not grounds to propose removing it.
No conflict with the SNA rejections (D-021, D-025, D-104..D-108). The paper makes no network, lobbying, or reciprocity claims.
Agent analysis in this note, including the assertiveness-split concern applied to text cues, is UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's note treats Birkenmaier & Lechner as the most direct transfer and names two weaknesses: converting traits into node parameters, and ambiguous statements. PoliPers is the facet framework underneath that codebook, and it sharpens his first worry. It defines facets and shows that their ratings are reliable only in part, but it says nothing about how a facet changes a politician's response to pressure. The trait-to-node conversion (communion susceptible, agency resistant) therefore remains unsupported by this whole literature line. His receptivity note that ten personalities collapse into four observable ones understates the reduction: PoliPers offers 15 facets, and the system uses 2. His notes are not stale, but they do not record that the codebook inherits PoliPers' unstable Assertiveness facet, or that observer-rated persona carries partisan bias.

related.why: Same author group. Birkenmaier & Lechner operationalize two PoliPers facets (Assertiveness/Agency and Empathy/Communion) as text cues, and that is the version the system's codebook ports.
Expert ratings of US senators are the system's gold panel. PoliPers shows that citizen observer ratings carry ideological-proximity bias, which motivates checking the panel for the same.
Ramey infers domain-level Big Five from speech. PoliPers argues domain-level measures lack political contextualization and favors facet-level, role-specific items.
Hierarchical facet-level inventory construction. PoliPers validates against the short BFI-2-XS version of this instrument.
The BFI-2-XS is the convergent-validity instrument in PoliPers Study 2 (the paper cites the 2018 German version).
PoliPers cites Amsalem et al. on politicians' personality and media visibility (lower A, higher E/ES/O more covered).

Byrne supplies the pressure mechanism the receptivity layer assumes. PoliPers supplies facet definitions but no pressure-response evidence, so the two together show the gap between construct and engine use.
